stops.name: Vikingsholm
stops.addr: Vikingsholm, Emerald Bay State Park, Highway 89, South Lake Tahoe, CA
stops.invite: A Scandinavian-style stone castle on Emerald Bay that took about 200 workers and one very determined summer resident.
story: Lora Josephine Knight built Vikingsholm as a summer home. She and her architect traveled to Scandinavia before construction, and the foundation was laid in 1928. About 200 workers finished it in 1929.
The architects were Lennart Palme and Matt Green. Some parts contain no nails or spikes, and most materials were local.

California bought the land from the lumberman Harvey West in 1953, for half its appraised value. Vikingsholm is part of Emerald Bay State Park and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1996. Knight's teahouse sits on Fannette Island in the bay, and you can only reach it by boat.

facts.t: Lora Josephine Knight built Vikingsholm as a summer home.
The foundation was laid in 1928 and about 200 workers completed the building in 1929.
The architects were Lennart Palme and Matt Green.
California bought the land from Harvey West in 1953 for half its appraised value.
It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on October 10, 1996.
The state park describes it as a Scandinavian-style castle, and the hike down is steep, about two miles round trip.

stops.access: Vikingsholm sits at the bottom of a steep trail from the Highway 89 lot, with no rides back up. State Parks says to skip the hike if you have medical or mobility concerns. Tours are run by the Sierra State Parks Foundation, first come first served, seasonally. Check the park page for current dates before you go.

access_check.how: Story read against Wikipedia and the California State Parks Emerald Bay page; tour season text there was for 2026 and may change. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Pope Estate at Tallac
stops.addr: Tallac Historic Site, 1 Heritage Way, South Lake Tahoe, CA 96150
stops.invite: A shingled summer estate from Tahoe's grand-resort era, now a free-to-wander historic site with seasonal tours.
story: The Pope Estate is a summer home in the Tallac Historic Site, a cluster of three lakeside estates. The Tevis family owned it, and Wikipedia describes its builder as Lloyd Tevis, a former president of Wells Fargo Bank. Sources disagree on the date: one gives the 1880s, and the site's own page gives 1894.

It is built entirely of wood with shingle siding, and the grounds include servants' cabins. George A. Pope of the Talbot and Pope Lumber company bought the home in 1923, and the Pope family sold it in 1965.

Next door, Elias J. "Lucky" Baldwin bought land here in 1872 and finished a big Tallac Hotel in 1899. His daughter Anita had the hotel demolished in 1920. The Tallac Historic Site went onto the National Register of Historic Places in 1987.

facts.t: The Pope Estate is a shingle-sided wooden home with servants' cabins on the grounds.
The Tevis family owned the property, and Baldwin sold it to them in 1899.
George A. Pope bought the home in 1923, and the Pope family sold it in 1965.
Wikipedia says the home was built in the 1880s; the Tallac site says 1894.
Elias J. Baldwin bought the remaining 138 acres in 1872 and completed the Tallac Hotel in 1899.
Anita Baldwin demolished the Tallac Hotel in 1920.
The estate was added to the National Register of Historic Places on April 1, 1987.
Guided tours and programs run seasonally, May through October, and have fees.

stops.access: The site is at 1 Heritage Way. The museum was closed for the season when checked, but parking, trails and restrooms stay open. Guided Pope House tours run seasonally from May through October for a fee, so check with the Tallac Museum before planning around a tour.

access_check.how: Story and access read against Wikipedia's Pope Estate page and the Taylor-Tallac Association's site pages; tour dates change by season. Not walked yet.

ph.alt: The Pope Estate, a shingled lakeside house among tall pines

stops.name: Chapel of the Transfiguration
stops.addr: 855 West Lake Blvd, Tahoe City, CA 96145
stops.invite: A rough-stone outdoor chapel built in a single summer in 1909, with pews outside and doors that open to the pines.
story: The Bliss family donated two acres in 1908, and Robert Montgomery Watson and his youngest son built the chapel during the summer of 1909. They used rough rubble stone, peeled logs and a steep shingled roof.
The National Register nomination credits the architects Walter Danforth Bliss and William Faville. It is a small building, about 676 square feet, with a stone altar at the front.
It served summer congregations, and weddings were held there. The chapel was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

facts.t: The Bliss family donated the land in 1908, and construction took place in summer 1909.
Robert Montgomery Watson and his youngest son, Robert H. Watson, built the chapel.
The nomination credits Walter Danforth Bliss and William Faville as architects.
The building is about 676 square feet, with rubble stone walls and a stone altar.
It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on August 18, 2011.
It was used for summer services and weddings.

stops.access: The chapel is at 855 West Lake Boulevard. It is an outdoor chapel used for services, so be quiet and respectful, and check with the church before going if you want to see the inside or if a service might be on.

access_check.how: Story read against the National Register nomination, a local history page and Wikipedia; no hours were found, so a visit time is not stated. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Old Truckee Jail
stops.invite: A stone-and-brick jail that ran from 1875 to 1964, which is a long time to keep people in one small building.
story: Construction began on August 11, 1875, and the jail was ready for use on September 22. The contract went to James Stewart, described as Truckee's premier stonemason, with a bid of $1,235 not counting the ironwork.

It was used continuously until May 1964. The historical society says Baby Face Nelson and Ma Spinelli and her gang were held here. Old-timers say Machine Gun Kelly spent a night after a shoplifting arrest, but that is a story, not a confirmed fact.
Today it is the Old Jail Museum, run by the Truckee-Donner Historical Society.

facts.t: Construction began August 11, 1875, and the jail was ready September 22, 1875.
The contract went to the stonemason James Stewart, with a bid of $1,235 not counting the ironwork.
The jail was used continuously from 1875 until May 1964.
Baby Face Nelson and Ma Spinelli's gang are listed as prisoners; the Machine Gun Kelly overnight stay is an unconfirmed local story.
The address is 10142 Jibboom Street.
An E Clampus Vitus plaque was put up in 1966 and re-dedicated July 4, 1978.

stops.access: The museum is generally open on summer weekends and is run by volunteers, so openings depend on who is available. The historical society's page gives two different sets of hours, so check its calendar or call (530) 582-0893 before you go. You can see the outside any time.

access_check.how: Story read against the Truckee-Donner Historical Society's page and NoeHill; the hours are inconsistent on the society's own page, so none are stated. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Truckee Train Depot
stops.invite: A depot built after the hotel that held the old station burned down, still meeting trains on the first transcontinental line.
story: After the transcontinental railroad was finished in 1869, Truckee's passenger depot and ticket office moved into the ground floor of J. F. Moody's Truckee Hotel. The hotel burned in early spring 1900.

The present depot went up that summer. The historical society says it follows Southern Pacific's standard One Story Combination Depot No. 23 design. A second source dates it only to around 1900, so treat the exact year as approximate.
Nevada County bought and remodeled the station in 1985. Today it is a transportation center, with the Amtrak California Zephyr, buses, a visitor information room and a local history museum.

facts.t: After 1869 the passenger depot moved into the ground floor of J. F. Moody's Truckee Hotel, which burned in early spring 1900.
The present depot was built in the summer of 1900 (the other source says around 1900).
It follows Southern Pacific's standard One Story Combination Depot No. 23 design.
It was placed on the California List of Historic Landmarks in 1976.
Nevada County bought and remodeled it in 1985, and it is now a transportation center with Amtrak, buses, a visitor room and a museum.
The address is 10065 Donner Pass Road, and it contributes to the Brickelltown Historic District.

stops.access: A working station at 10065 Donner Pass Road. Amtrak's California Zephyr stops here, so be careful around the tracks and platform. The visitor room and museum have their own hours, which were not confirmed, so check with the Truckee-Donner Historical Society.

access_check.how: Story read against the Truckee-Donner Historical Society's depot page and NoeHill; the build year differs slightly between them and is worded as approximate. Not walked yet.

sources.t: Truckee-Donner Historical Society: Truckee Train Depot

stops.name: Donner Memorial State Park
stops.invite: A state park around the Donner Party's winter camp, with a 1918 pioneer monument and a visitor center that tells more than one story.
story: Ninety people were in the Donner Party in the winter of 1846 to 1847, and 42 of them died, mostly from starvation and exposure.

The Pioneer Monument was dedicated on June 6, 1918, and the Native Sons of the Golden West built it. The state lists it as California Historical Landmark 134. The pedestal is 22 feet high, and the statue adds about 17.5 feet.

The visitor center opened on June 6, 2015, and replaced the Emigrant Trail Museum from 1962. State Parks says its exhibits also cover the Washoe people, Chinese railroad workers and early motoring over Donner Pass.

facts.t: Ninety people were in the Donner Party in 1846 to 1847, and 42 died, mostly of starvation and exposure.
The Pioneer Monument was dedicated June 6, 1918; the pedestal is 22 feet and the statue adds 17.5 feet.
The monument was built in 1918 by the Native Sons of the Golden West and is California Historical Landmark 134.
The visitor center opened June 6, 2015, replacing the 1962 Emigrant Trail Museum.
Exhibits cover the Donner Party, the Washoe people, Chinese railroad workers and early motoring over Donner Pass.
The park was established in 1928.
State Parks lists the visitor center as open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and day-use parking at $10 per vehicle.

stops.access: A state park at 12593 Donner Pass Road. State Parks lists the visitor center as open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. (closed Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's Day) and day-use parking at $10 per vehicle, from a 2024 info sheet. Check the State Parks page for current hours and fees. This is the site of a real tragedy, so treat it quietly.
